summary: Describes models for deploying DNSSEC when an enterprise uses several DNS providers for its authoritative service. Difficulties can arise depending on features in use, especially when each provider signs the zone with its own keys. It is informational.

eli5.summary: If two companies each print the same signed notice with their own stamp, readers may be confused about which stamp to trust. This document describes the setups that let a name be served by several providers without breaking trust.

questions: how to use dnssec with multiple dns providers
what is a combined signing key
how do key rollovers work with multiple dns providers
subtitle: How to run DNSSEC when two or more DNS providers each sign the same zone with their own keys.

tldr.problem: Enterprises use several DNS providers for redundancy, but when each provider signs the zone with its own keys, a validating resolver can get a signature it cannot check against the keys it already cached.
tldr.mechanism: Two models are described. In both, every provider's DNSKEY RRset contains the zone signing keys of all providers. In Model 1 the zone owner holds one common KSK; in Model 2 each provider has its own KSK and the parent holds a DS record for each.
tldr.outcome: Resolvers need no changes, but the zone owner must coordinate key rollovers and providers need APIs to import and export keys. This is an Informational document.

facts.label: Models
facts.value: 2 (common KSK, or unique KSK per provider)

today: RFC 8901 is an Informational document, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It describes deployment models and does not change how validating resolvers behave.

sections.title: Why Several Providers Sign One Zone
sections.content:
Many enterprises use more than one DNS provider for their authoritative service. This is mainly for redundancy and availability, so that the service survives a catastrophic failure of any single provider.

If standard zone-transfer techniques can be used, nothing special is needed: a single entity signs, and the providers act as secondary servers. Sometimes, though, zone transfer cannot be used. The zone may rely on nonstandard DNS features, or a provider may only support online signing (signing answers on the fly). Then each provider acts like a primary server and signs the data with its own keys. This document describes models for that case and the key-management requirements they bring.
sections.eli5: Having two helpers means the service keeps working if one of them breaks. The tricky part comes when both helpers sign their answers with different pens.

sections.title: The Two Multi-Signer Models
sections.content:
The zone owner updates zone content the same way at every provider, usually through provider-specific APIs, and each provider signs. The key rule is that each provider imports the public Zone Signing Keys (ZSKs) of all the other providers into its DNSKEY RRset. The providers are not expected to talk to each other directly, since they usually only have a contract with the zone owner.

Model 1: common KSK set, unique ZSK set per provider. The zone owner holds the Key Signing Key (KSK) set, manages the DS records and signs the combined DNSKEY RRset, then distributes it to the providers. Each provider signs zone data with its own ZSK. The zone owner must re-sign the DNSKEY RRset periodically as signatures near expiry.

Model 2: unique KSK set and ZSK set per provider. Each provider has its own KSK and ZSK and signs the DNSKEY RRset with its own KSK. The zone owner imports each provider's ZSKs into the others and manages a DS RRset in the parent zone with a DS record for each provider's KSK.

A Combined Signing Key (CSK) is a single key with no KSK/ZSK split. Model 1 cannot use CSKs, because the owner would hold the only signing key. Model 2 can.
sections.eli5: In the first setup, one boss signs the master list of trusted pens. In the second, each helper signs their own list, and the boss tells the parent about each helper.

sections.title: What Validating Resolvers See
sections.content:
The reason every provider must publish all the ZSKs is how resolvers cache. A resolver may fetch and validate the DNSKEY RRset from Provider A, cache it, and later ask Provider B for an answer. If Provider B signs with a ZSK that is missing from the cached RRset, the resolver rejects the answer. It may then try other nameservers until it reaches one of Provider A's, which costs extra round trips. It may even give up, or its own clients may time out.

Keeping every provider's DNSKEY RRset populated with all active ZSKs means a resolver can validate no matter which provider answered. In Model 1 the one KSK signs an identical DNSKEY RRset at each provider. In Model 2 the parent's DS RRset has several DS records, one per provider KSK. In both cases the resolver needs no new behavior.
sections.eli5: If a reader remembers only one helper's list of real pens, a note signed by the other helper looks fake. Both lists must name every pen.

sections.title: Algorithms and Authenticated Denial
sections.content:
Providers need a common signing algorithm, or a common set of algorithms. The specifications require that when a DNSKEY RRset has several algorithms, every RRset is signed with at least one key of each algorithm (RFC 4035, Section 2.2), which providers using different algorithms could not satisfy.

Authenticated denial of existence uses signed NSEC or NSEC3 records to prove a name does not exist. These responses are self-contained, so no rollover is needed when switching between them, and different providers can use different methods. However, mixing NSEC with NSEC3 defeats the zone-enumeration protection of NSEC3. The RFC prefers using a single method everywhere. If that is impossible, it recommends keeping the number of distinct configurations as low as possible, and it notes that mixed setups can make negative caching less efficient. NSEC3 on all providers with different NSEC3PARAM values counts as mixed.
sections.eli5: All the helpers must write in the same alphabet. When they say that something does not exist, they should all use the same kind of proof, or readers get confused.

sections.title: Key Rollovers and CDS/CDNSKEY
sections.content:
Rollovers need coordination between providers and the zone owner. The RFC assumes two providers, the Double-Signature KSK method and the Pre-Publish ZSK method from RFC 6781, and suggests the zone owner start rollovers, although a provider could signal its intent instead.

  • Model 1 KSK roll: the owner generates a new KSK, adds it to each provider's DNSKEY RRset, signs with both old and new KSK, and pushes the result. The owner then changes the DS RRset in the parent and, after the DS TTL, removes the old KSK.
  • Model 1 ZSK roll: the provider announces a new ZSK. Because the owner signs the RRset, the owner inserts the key into every provider's RRset, re-signs and redistributes it, and later removes the old key.
  • Model 2 KSK roll: the provider adds a new KSK and signs with both. The owner replaces the DS record in the parent. The old KSK is removed after the DS TTL.
  • Model 2 ZSK roll: the provider adds a new ZSK, the owner imports it into the other providers, and the provider waits for the DNSKEY TTL, import time and propagation before signing with it.

CDS and CDNSKEY records can automate parent updates. In Model 1 they are handled by the zone owner. In Model 2 the key-management mechanism must cross-import them so every provider shows the same view to the parent.
sections.eli5: Changing a stamp is a team job. The boss and the helpers must take turns, so that at every moment readers can still check the stamps in use.

sections.title: Provider APIs, Response Size and Security
sections.content:
The RFC does not define a new API. It lists what a provider's own API (often HTTPS and REST) must be able to do. All providers must offer a way to query the current DNSKEY RRset. For Model 1, the API must import a signed DNSKEY RRset (and a signed CDS/CDNSKEY RRset if supported). For Model 2, it must import a DNSKEY record from another provider (and individual CDS/CDNSKEY records).

Multi-signer setups make the DNSKEY RRset larger. The RFC says newer elliptic-curve keys are small enough that responses typically stay far below the common path MTU, but operators still need to handle large UDP responses.

Security-wise, third-party providers hold private signing keys, so the zone owner places a great deal of trust in them. The RFC says the traditional hidden-master setup with zone transfer is arguably more secure. Key import and export APIs must be strongly authenticated, for example with multifactor authentication, or TSIG for DNS UPDATE.
sections.eli5: Each helper needs a safe door where the boss can ask for, or hand over, the list of trusted pens. That door must have a good lock.
